prize_parts.citation: for establishing that biomolecular condensates form by phase separation, a physical-chemical principle of intracellular organisation

statement.case_for: Biomolecular phase separation introduced a genuinely new concept of molecular organisation: membraneless compartments behave as condensed phases whose formation follows from multivalency, sequence-encoded interactions, thermodynamics and phase behaviour. Hyman and Brangwynne showed in 2009 that P granules are liquid droplets, and Rosen's multivalent-interaction work supplied the quantitative phase-diagram framework. The idea reduces a messy cellular phenomenon to general physical-chemical principles, has been taken up across biophysics, cell biology and neurodegeneration research, and ties directly to lipid, protein and amyloid self-assembly. It is chemistry in the sense of intermolecular forces and phases, not just cell biology.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the field is still contested on physiological relevance: many reported condensates were seen in vitro or with overexpression, and the functional significance of the material state is unresolved. There is also a real question whether the Medicine/Physiology community is the more natural home, and credit between experimental discovery (Hyman, Brangwynne) and theory/sequence grammar (Rosen, Pappu, Mittag) cannot be cut cleanly into three. The committee could fairly judge this too early or too diffuse, and only I ranked it first, so I should not mistake my own field's enthusiasm for committee-wide merit.

responses.point: Aili ranks PROTACs and molecular glues (B068) first as a designable chemical handle on the ubiquitin-proteasome system, with many degraders in the clinic and Crews, Deshaies and Handa as the core.
responses.response: I accept this as a real chemical design principle and the strongest case from the chemical-biology side, and I moved it up in my own thinking from my low opening rank. My reservations are that no PROTAC drug is approved yet, and that the PROTAC and cereblon-glue strands (Crews/Deshaies versus Handa/Ito) are separate discoveries, so a three-name prize either splits two achievements or leaves out one. I would call it a serious second choice rather than my first, and I would like to hear whether he sees the clinical gap as a real obstacle.

responses.point: Somfai places Buchwald-Hartwig C-N coupling (B011) first as the clearest case of a method that changed how chemists build bonds everywhere, with a clean two-person attribution and recognition arguably overdue.
responses.response: I agree on the merits of B011: its attribution is cleaner than almost anything else on the shortlist, and the maturity concern is the opposite of mine for B019. I am not arguing it is less worthy. My question is one of balance: it is the third or fourth synthetic-methodology prize in a short period, and I do not want to equate the breadth of opening support, four members including two first places, with greater scientific novelty than a new organising principle. I would not oppose it as part of a two-part prize, and I would value his view on whether Kosugi's tin-amide precedent weakens the two-name citation.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks long-range electron transfer through proteins (B053, Gray and Winkler) first as a quantitative, physically grounded mechanism underpinning respiration and photosynthesis.
responses.response: As a physical chemist I respect the tunnelling-versus-distance framework, and it is exactly the kind of mechanism-in-physical-terms I like. But I share his own concern that the field is old and Marcus's 1992 prize already covered the theoretical core, so the incremental recognition value looks lower than for a new concept. I also doubt it can compete in a majority vote since nobody else ranked it, so I would ask him whether he would pair it with something rather than push it alone.

responses.point: Linke ranks the dye-sensitized solar cell (B039, Gratzel and O'Regan) first as a kinetically clear, long-validated interface principle and puts nanopore sequencing and massively parallel sequencing next.
responses.response: I find the interfacial-kinetics argument for B039 convincing and the maturity unquestionable. I would distinguish it from B019 on novelty of concept versus clarity of an engineering step, but I accept that is arguable. I disagree with his caution that PROTACs are somewhat early only mildly, and I would add that the same maturity yardstick he applies there should also be applied to condensates, which are younger still, so I am not claiming a standard I fail to meet myself.

responses.point: Chabes ranks PROTACs first and massively parallel sequencing second, valuing a general tool and a measured impact in genomes sequenced.
responses.response: The sequencing impact is undisputed, but I am not persuaded it is as new chemically as the reversible-terminator step is claimed to be, and credit among competing platforms (Solexa, 454, Mayer, Ju) is contested. I would want to hear how he would limit the names without leaving out a decisive lineage.

uncertainties: Whether in-cell phase separation is established enough, as opposed to in vitro behaviour, to justify a Chemistry prize now.
Whether a three-name condensate prize can be drawn cleanly among Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen, Pappu and Mittag.

Whether the committee prefers B063 (lipid nanoparticles) because of validated impact, given overlap with the 2023 Medicine prize and the unresolved allocation among Cullis, MacLachlan and Anderson/Langer.
Whether the clinical gap for PROTACs should defer B068, and how to treat PROTAC and cereblon-glue strands.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. I share Lund University with Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, and my work on lipids and amyloid is thematically close to B019 and B063 and overlaps with Brzezinski and Aili on membranes and self-assembly. These are field proximities rather than personal ties to any candidate named, and I have no recorded collaboration with any listed candidate.
